newsitem.title: FRANCE: Russia's Lebed ends French tour, warns of upheaval.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed ends French tour, warns of upheaval.

text.p: Presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed warned on Friday of the danger of social unrest in Russia, and pledged to crack down on corruption and crime and break the power of the oligarchy if he came to power.
"The situation in Russia is disgusting," said Lebed, who is seen as the presidential frontrunner if President Boris Yeltsin's faltering health forced new elections.
Unless "a civilised solution" was found, there could be a social explosion which would be hard to rein in, the 46-year-old army general told a news conference at the end of a five-day private visit.
"Hope has nearly died...There will be a solution by the end of this year, this is certain. There is no other way out," he said separately in an interview in the newspaper Le Monde.

Lebed proposed to attack corruption and crime, do away with the power of the oligarchy, share out power between the federal government and regions, and hold regional referenda on privatising land if he were to become president.
But he admitted that he was not yet clear on what to do after law and order is restored, although priorities should be to invest in science, high technology, culture and education.
"My task is to lay the first stone of the future democracy, place Russia on the road to social development," he said.
He said he had built up a political machine backing him in 32 regions of Russia. His supporters are political newcomers, he said, adding: "I do not play with used cards".

The centre-right French government, wary of repeating the blunder of a cool reception to Boris Yeltsin before he became president, greeted Lebed with all honours available to a distinguished private visitor.

Lebed met the speakers of both houses of parliament, the governor of the Bank of France, foreign ministry officials and the leader of the Socialist opposition. Newspapers and television fought for interviews.
He visited the grave of wartime leader General Charles de Gaulle, one of his personal heroes, but had to cancel a visit to the tomb of emperor Napoleon because of a painful in-grown toenail.
Lebed said he bore no grudge that President Jacques Chirac had not received him.
"I am a private citizen and I do not want to embarrass the president of France. One must enter a house when the doors are wide open, not through the window," he said.
He said he would study a suggestion that he set up a permanent office -- "a personal embassy" -- in Paris.

Standing with military stiffness through the 90-minute news conference in the ornate gilded hall of the Grand Hotel, the inscrutable 46-year-old general refused to be taken in by the French capital's elegant charm.
He admitted Paris was "a remarkable city" and the hotel was beautiful. But he added in his gravelly voice: "I try to be comfortable anywhere, here or in a soldier's foxhole".
Receiving a friendship medal from the Normandy port of Honfleur which is hosting a Russian film festival, he called it "my first peace award" after medals won on the battlefield.
Lebed, who recently visited Washington and Germany, said his trips to the West had not changed his vision of the world.
Then why all these trips? "Why would I reveal my most secret designs to you?" he answered.

Lebed said there was great potential for increased cooperation between Russia, France and Germany, and even suggested organising cultural competitions such as used to be staged between mediaeval troubadours.
